title: The Efficacy and Safety of Dalfampridine on Cognition and Fatigue in People With Multiple Sclerosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Halabi MH, Alromayan R, Almutairi M, Alasmari H, AlGhamdi MA, Makkawi S
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease affecting the central nervous system. People with MS frequently experience cognitive dysfunction and fatigue. Dalfampridine (DAL), a potassium channel blocker, is US Food and Drug Administration-approved for the treatment of walking impairment in people with MS. It may also enhance nerve conduction in regions associated with fatigue and cognitive dysfunction. This study aims to evaluate DAL's efficacy in improving these symptoms, as well as its safety profile, in people with MS. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted across MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science, covering all records from database inception through April 1, 2024. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing DAL with placebo in people with MS and reporting impaired cognition and fatigue were included. A random-effects model was used to calculate the risk ratio (RR), standardized mean difference (SMD), and mean difference (MD) with 95% CIs. RESULTS: Of 1329 studies identified, 13 RCTs involving a total of 827 people with MS were included. DAL demonstrated a significant improvement in cognitive symptoms (SMD = 0.21; 95% CI, 0.04-0.38; P = .01; I² = 6%). However, no significant difference was observed between DAL and placebo in reducing fatigue (MD = 3.70; 95% CI, -4.37 to 11.77;P = .37; I² = 19%). Safety measures were comparable, with no significant difference in adverse events (RR = 1.11; 95% CI, 0.99-1.25; P = .08; I² = 0%). CONCLUSIONS: People with MS receiving DAL demonstrated significant improvement in cognitive symptoms; however, further studies are warranted to validate and confirm this finding.

title: Exploring the therapeutic role of Chinses herbal medicine in the recurrence rate of uterine fibroids after conservative surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Liu Z, Liu Y, Li S, Zhang X, Qiang R, Jin F, Guo L, Hou T
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Since surgery can only remove lesions of a larger size visible to the naked eye, the recurrence rate of uterine fibroids after surgery is high. In recent years, numerous scholars have found that traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) treatment is effective in reducing the recurrence rate of postoperative fibroids, as well as improving the clinical treatment rate, regulating serum hormone levels, reducing plasma viscosity, and promoting the restoration of uterine volume following surgery. Several randomized controlled trials have been undertaken on the prevention and treatment of postoperative recurrence of uterine fibroids using patented Chinese medicines and self-proposed formulations, such as Guizhi Fuling Pill, Xiaozheng decoction, Xiangleng pill, Zhengjia decoction, Xiaoliu decoction, Guizhi Jiliu pill, Huoxue Huayu formula, Huoxue Xiaozheng decoction, Shugan Sanjie decoction, Gongliuxiao capsule, Hongjin Xiaojie concentrated pill, and Jiawei Guizhi Fuling decoction. However, no study has systematically evaluated Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) in reducing the recurrence rate of uterine fibroids after surgery. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to conduct a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of CHM for the prevention of postoperative recurrence of uterine fibroids, evaluating its efficacy and safety. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted on PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), VIP Information Database (VIP), WanFang Database, and China Biomedical Database (CBM) to identify randomized controlled clinical studies conducted up to March 2025 that examined the efficacy of CHM in treating patients with postoperative uterine fibroids. Two institutes were independently under-selected, and data were extracted and quality assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool. Meta-analyses were performed using Review Manager software 5.4, and forest plots were generated. The quality of evidence was assessed using GRADEpro 3.2.2. This study was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251000288). RESULTS: 16 trials were included in this study, and the postoperative recurrence rate after treatment was mainly analyzed. CHM treatment reduces postoperative recurrence rates in patients with uterine fibroids compared to the blank (6 trials, n = 588; OR (odds ratio) = 0.22; 95 % CI (95 % confidence intervals) = 0.14-0.34; I2 = 0 %, p < 0.00001), conventional western medicine (CWM) (1 trial, n = 80; OR = 0.30; 95 % CI = 0.09-0.93, p = 0.04), and combined CHM with CWM (9 trials, n = 959; OR = 0.29; 95 % CI = 0.19-0.46; I2 = 0 %, p < 0.00001). In addition, CHM is also effective in improving clinical efficiency, restoring serum sex hormone levels, lowering plasma viscosity, and reducing uterine volume. CHM is generally considered safe, with a low incidence of adverse reactions. CONCLUSION: CHM is effective in avoiding recurrence of uterine fibroids after surgery, excelling in terms of overall effectiveness, restoring female hormone levels, improving hemorheological indices, and promoting uterine recovery and safety. However, these findings are preliminary and still need to be validated by higher-quality studies.

title: Normothermic regional perfusion versus direct procurement with machine perfusion in donation after circulatory death heart transplantation: A systematic review and meta-analysis of early and mid-term outcomes.
authors: AlGhamdi M, Lebreton G, Rao V, Cusimano RJ, Leprince P
abstract: BACKGROUND: Donation after circulatory death (DCD) is now a major source of cardiac allografts, yet the two dominant recovery strategies, thoraco-abdominal normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) and direct procurement with ex-situ machine perfusion (DP-MP), have never been compared in a dedicated meta-analysis of clinically meaningful endpoints. METHODS: We systematically searched five databases and grey literature for studies comparing NRP with DP-MP in adult DCD heart transplantation. Random-effects models generated pooled risk ratios (RR), with Hartung-Knapp sensitivity analyses. The primary outcome was severe primary graft dysfunction (PGD); secondary outcomes were survival, treated acute cellular rejection (ACR) and cost. Risk of bias and certainty were assessed with ROBINS-I and GRADE. RESULTS: Eight studies were included, three pooled for PGD. NRP was associated with less severe PGD (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.25-0.60; n = 728; Hartung-Knapp 0.25-0.59) and less treated ACR at one year (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.35-0.76). Overlapping registry cohorts were de-duplicated; 30-day survival did not differ (RR 1.02, 95% CI 1.00-1.04; P = 0.073), and a borderline one-year difference (RR 1.04, 95% CI 1.00-1.08) was not robust to registry substitution, indicating equivalent survival. Cost favoured NRP; certainty was moderate. CONCLUSIONS: In adult DCD heart transplantation, thoraco-abdominal NRP was associated with lower rates of severe PGD and treated acute cellular rejection, at equivalent survival and lower cost. As the data are observational, these estimates remain imprecise and subject to residual confounding. NRP is reasonable where feasible, and adequately powered trials with standardised adjudication of graft dysfunction are needed.

title: H-shaped sponge positioner prevents pressure injuries during prolonged prone ventilation in acute respiratory distress syndrome: a single-center, open-label, randomized controlled trial.
authors: Wang Y, Liu J, Chen S, Tian S, Hu S, Tang B, Zeng L, Luo L
abstract: In patients with moderate-to-severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, prolonged prone position ventilation is frequently employed to enhance oxygenation but often results in pressure injuries. To protect patients from such injuries, a new H-shaped sponge locator was designed in the study. In this single-center, open-label, randomized controlled trial, 60 patients with moderate-to-severe acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring extended prone position ventilation (≥ 12 hours per session) were recruited from the General Intensive Care Unit at Xiangtan Central Hospital, Hunan Province, China, between May 2023 and May 2024. Participants were randomly allocated to either the intervention group, which received prone positioning with the assistance of the H-shaped sponge positioner, or the control group, which used conventional soft pillows for support. The primary outcomes included the number of anatomical sites affected by pressure injuries and injury severity, classified according to the revised 2016 National Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel/the European Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel staging criteria. Secondary outcomes included mean airway pressure, oxygenation index (PaO2/FiO2), intravesical pressure, and the frequency of support device adjustments. Data from 29 patients in each group were analyzed. Significant group × time interactions were observed for both the number of pressure injury sites and overall incidence. Although pressure injuries increased progressively across all sessions in both groups, patients in the intervention group consistently had fewer injury sites. There were no significant group × time interactions for mean airway pressure or intravesical pressure. However, both measures increased over time in all patients, with significantly lower values in the intervention group. Oxygenation index improved over time, with no statistically significant differences between groups. The intervention group required markedly fewer support device adjustments. In patients with moderate-to-severe acute respiratory distress syndrome receiving extended prone position ventilation, the H-shaped sponge positioner significantly outperformed standard soft pillow support in preventing pressure injuries. This cost-efficient device not only minimized the number and severity of pressure ulcers but also reduced mean airway and intra-abdominal pressures and decreased the frequency of nursing interventions. Given its ease of use and affordability, the H-shaped positioner holds substantial promise for clinical application, particularly in resource-constrained settings, and warrants further evaluation in broader implementation studies. This trial was registred at National Health Security Information Platform (Medical Research Registration and Information System, https://www.medicalresearch.org.cn, Registration No. MR-43-23-039592) on March 30, 2023.

title: Prospective Multicenter Evaluation of a Novel Low-Axial-Force Colonic Stent for Malignant Colorectal Obstruction.
authors: Otsuka R, Saito S, Fujimoto N, Hanabata N, Takao A, Narita K, Kuwai T, Endo S
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Self-expandable metal stents (SEMSs) are used as a bridge to surgery (BTS) or for palliation (PAL) in malignant colorectal obstruction, but high axial force may contribute to perforation. We prospectively evaluated the efficacy and safety of the low-axial-force Naturfit colonic stent in both settings. METHODS: This prospective multicenter single-arm study enrolled 208 patients at 11 Japanese institutions between 2019 and 2022 (BTS, n = 137; PAL, n = 71). The primary endpoint was clinical success of colorectal stenting; secondary endpoints included technical success, adverse events, surgical outcomes after BTS stenting, and 12-month palliative outcomes. RESULTS: Technical success and clinical success of colorectal stenting were both 99.0%, with perforation in three patients (1.4%). In the BTS cohort, clinical success of BTS was 97.1%; no perforations occurred, and early and late adverse-event rates were 1.5% and 3.7%. All patients underwent elective surgery; colostomy and laparoscopic surgery rates were 4.4% and 87.6%. In the palliative cohort, clinical success of colorectal stenting was 98.6%, late adverse events occurred in 16.9%, and 12-month overall survival and stent patency were 46.6% and 67.6%. CONCLUSIONS: Naturfit achieved high technical and clinical success of colorectal stenting with a low perforation rate. These findings support its feasibility for malignant colorectal obstruction in both BTS and palliative settings, although comparative studies are needed to determine relative advantages over other SEMSs. TRIAL REGISTRATION: University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trial Registry: UMIN000035224.

title: Modern cell-based assays for biomedical research: from conventional methods to AI-driven high content analysis.
authors: Venkataramaiah C
abstract: In vitro cell-based assays are fundamental tools in biomedical research, supporting investigations of cellular physiology, disease mechanisms, drug discovery, toxicology, regenerative medicine, and precision therapeutics. However, conventional two-dimensional (2D) cell culture models often fail to recapitulate the structural complexity and physiological functions of native tissues, prompting the development of advanced platforms, including three-dimensional (3D) cultures, organoids, organ-on-a-chip technologies, and microphysiological systems. Recent advances in cell viability and cytotoxicity assessment, functional cellular analysis, molecular profiling, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based functional genomics, high-content imaging, flow cytometry, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and automated high-throughput screening have expanded the analytical capabilities of cell-based assays. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted image analysis and computational biology has enhanced cellular phenotyping, biomarker discovery, and mechanistic investigation, with the potential to improve the prediction of therapeutic efficacy and toxicity. Nevertheless, challenges related to physiological relevance, technical variability, inadequate standardization, high operational costs, scalability, poor reproducibility, cell-line misidentification, batch-to-batch variation, and inconsistent reporting continue to hinder translational applications. Future progress will depend on integrating physiologically relevant models with AI-driven analytics, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, automated screening, and microphysiological systems. Standardized protocols, harmonized reporting practices, and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to improve reproducibility, strengthen regulatory acceptance, advance precision medicine, and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. In this context, this review critically evaluates conventional and emerging in vitro cell-based assays, emphasizing their biological principles, analytical capabilities, translational applications, and practical limitations, while highlighting future opportunities to improve predictive accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical translation.

title: Next-generation anti-obesity drugs: emerging molecular targets and translational opportunities.
authors: Shetty S, Rangle A, Mukherjee AG, Bharti AK, Jena SP, Prince SE, Gopalakrishnan AV
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: PURPOSE: Obesity is a heterogeneous, chronic metabolic disease driven by dysregulation of energy homeostasis across interconnected central nervous system, gastrointestinal, adipose, endocrine, immune, and mitochondrial networks. Despite the established roles of lifestyle intervention and metabolic/bariatric surgery, limitations in accessibility, durability, and interindividual response have stimulated the development of mechanism-based pharmacotherapies. This review critically examines emerging therapeutic strategies targeting integrated energy-regulatory pathways and evaluates their translational potential for precision obesity management. METHODS: Current evidence was synthesized across major biological systems governing appetite, energy expenditure, and metabolic adaptation. Central melanocortin, Neuropeptide Y (NPY)/ Agouti-related peptide (AgRP), serotonergic, dopaminergic, and endocannabinoid pathways were considered alongside gut-derived incretin, amylin, Peptide YY (PYY), ghrelin, Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF), and bile acid signaling. Emerging approaches targeting adipose remodeling, thermogenesis, mitochondrial energetics, AMPK-mTOR-sirtuin signaling, inflammation, and fibrosis were also evaluated. Genetic, epigenetic, and artificial intelligence-based approaches to patient stratification were incorporated to assess prospects for precision therapy. RESULTS: Obesity pharmacotherapy is shifting from conventional appetite suppression toward coordinated modulation of interconnected metabolic pathways. Incretin-based and multi-agonist therapies provide the strongest clinical evidence for substantial weight reduction and metabolic improvement. However, treatment discontinuation, weight regain, adverse effects, cost, and heterogeneous therapeutic responses remain major challenges. Strategies targeting adipose tissue dysfunction, mitochondrial metabolism, thermogenesis, immune-metabolic signaling, and fibrosis offer additional opportunities for disease modification, although many remain in preclinical or early clinical development. Increasing evidence for biological heterogeneity supports individualized therapeutic selection. CONCLUSION: The emerging therapeutic paradigm positions obesity as a systems-level disorder requiring mechanism-informed, individualized intervention. Integrating CNS-gut-adipose-mitochondrial biology with multi-omics, biomarkers, and artificial intelligence may enable more durable and precise treatment. Long-term safety, durability, affordability, equitable access, and clinical validation remain essential for translation.

title: Consent for intensive care research involving adults who lack decision-making capacity: A jurisdictional analysis of Australia's fragmented framework.
authors: Bihari S, Galluccio S, McIntyre J, Plummer M, Nair P, Saxena M, Buhr H, Neto AS
journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
abstract: Critically ill adults frequently cannot consent to research because of sedation, delirium, shock or mechanical ventilation, yet safe intensive care depends on evidence generated in this population; several treatments once regarded as standard care proved harmful when finally tested in randomised trials. The ethical framework for enrolling adults who lack decision-making capacity is national-the National Health and Medical Research Council National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (2025), in effect since 23 June 2026-but legal authority for substitute consent is conferred by eight state and territory statutes that differ in terminology, in decision-maker hierarchies, in whether they address research at all, and whether they permit enrolment in an emergency. Mapping four representative study archetypes across all eight jurisdictions shows that the lawful basis for enrolling the same patient shifts with study design as much as with geography; differing statutory definitions, tribunal involvement and the transition to the 2025 National Statement produce material and avoidable inconsistency. Contemporary Australian intensive care trials show that practice has converged on the National Statement while the underlying legislation has not; the resulting inconsistency risks inequity, underrepresentation of critically ill patients, and bias in the evidence generated. We set out principles for reform (Box 1): nationally consistent framing of substitute consent for research-common terminology and legal principles, an explicit emergency-research pathway in every jurisdiction, and consistent interpretation within each jurisdiction-developed with consumers and with the clinicians and clinical research nurses who obtain consent, and taken forward with formal endorsement from the relevant professional bodies.

title: Kidney effects of inhaled nitric oxide in critically ill patients: from pathophysiological considerations to clinical implications.
authors: Robert A, Gonze A, Bulpa P, Hauquiert B
abstract: Inhaled nitric oxide is widely used as a selective pulmonary vasodilator in critical care, yet its renal effects remain controversial. While existing reviews mostly focus on indications for inhaled nitric oxide and its impact on outcomes, limited data exist on its renal effects, since it was thought to act only locally in the lungs. This review examine the clinical evidence regarding kidney outcomes associated with inhaled nitric oxide across major indications and provide an integrated mechanistic analysis of nitric oxide signaling in renal physiology and pathophysiology. Nitric oxide is produced by nitric oxide synthases using L-arginine as a substrate. It acts as a smooth muscle relaxation factor and ultimately causes vasodilation through its effect on cyclic guanosine monophosphate. Nitric oxide plays a pivotal role in renal hemodynamic regulation, glomerular filtration, tubular function, and microcirculatory homeostasis. The net renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide likely reflects the balance between improved nitric oxide signaling and oxidative stress generation. Available clinical data suggest that the renal impact of inhaled nitric oxide is context-dependent. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, higher-level evidence indicates a potential increase in acute kidney injury, possibly related to oxidative and nitrosative stress. Conversely, in cardiac bypass surgery, inhaled nitric oxide may confer nephroprotection by restoring nitric oxide bioavailability during hemolysis and free hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging. In other conditions, including organ transplantation, pulmonary hypertension, sepsis, and hemolytic disorders, evidence remains limited or inconclusive. Overall, current evidence does not support a uniform renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide, indicating the need for prospective studies with predefined renal endpoints to clarify its clinical relevance.

title: Environmental microbial exposure as an under-measured exposome domain: Links to host microbiomes, immune regulation, and disease epidemiology.
authors: Parekh Y, Parmar V
journal: Journal of environmental health science & engineering
abstract: Environmental microbial exposure is an under-measured biological component of the exposome and a plausible determinant of immune-mediated disease patterns. Humans encounter microbial communities and products from soil, air, water, vegetation, animals, food systems, farms, indoor dust, healthcare settings, schools, and urban built environments. These exposures may influence gut, skin, airway, oral, and mucosal microbiomes and thereby alter epithelial barrier function, immune tolerance, inflammatory thresholds, and microbial metabolite production. This structured mechanistic narrative review integrates direct environmental-exposure studies, environment-to-host microbiome studies, host-microbiome mechanistic evidence, and translational frameworks. The clearest convergence occurs in asthma and allergic disease, where early-life farm exposure, endotoxin-rich dust, environmental microbial diversity, innate immune modulation, and epithelial A20 regulation support a coherent exposure-response model. Evidence for inflammatory bowel disease and broader respiratory outcomes is biologically credible but less direct, whereas metabolic and systemic inflammatory outcomes remain largely supported by host-microbiome and metabolite mechanisms rather than direct environmental exposure studies. The review therefore distinguishes evidence maturity and mechanistic proximity rather than treating all disease categories equally. It further positions pollution, urbanization, building design, biodiversity loss, diet, antibiotics, and socioeconomic conditions as active modifiers of microbial exposure and host response. Future studies should integrate direct environmental sampling with body-site microbiome profiling, functional multi-omics, immune and barrier biomarkers, geospatial exposure assessment, source tracking, repeated measures, and explicit causal-inference designs. Environmental microbial exposure should be treated neither as uniformly beneficial nor harmful, but as a measurable, context-dependent exposome domain whose health effects depend on composition, dose, timing, route, co-exposures, and host susceptibility.

title: Understanding diabetes through social determinants of health: An umbrella review in the Eastern Mediterranean Region.
authors: Jafarzadeh J, Mohamadi E, Namazi N, Yaftian F, Mostafavi H, Noorimotlagh Z, Bakhtiari A, Olyaeemanesh A
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetes is a main public health concern in the Eastern Mediterranean Region, where social determinants of health are associated with disease occurrence, diagnosis, self-management, complications, and quality of life. Although several reviews have examined diabetes in this region, differences in their scopes, methods, quality, and reporting have limited a consolidated understanding of the social determinants associated with the disease. This umbrella review synthesized evidence from existing reviews on diabetes related social determinants across Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) countries using an ICD-10 Z-code framework. METHODS: PubMed and Scopus were searched for review articles published between January 2000 and April 21, 2025. Eligible reviews included narrative reviews, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, and scoping reviews that examined social or economic determinants of diabetes in human populations from EMR countries. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through consensus or third reviewer adjudication. Methodological quality was assessed using SANRA for narrative reviews and CAT HPPR for systematic, meta-analytic, and scoping reviews. Extracted determinants were synthesized through conceptual mapping to ICD-10 Z-codes Z55 to Z65 and Z70 to Z76. RESULTS: Of 119 retrieved records, 55 reviews met the inclusion criteria. Reviews were published between 2000 and 2025 and most commonly covered Saudi Arabia, Iran, and Pakistan. The core synthesis identified 343 reported occurrences of social determinants of health mapped to ICD-10 Z55-Z65, with housing and economic circumstances and the social environment most frequently reported. A separate contextual synthesis described 262 Z70-Z76 findings related to behavioural pathways, life-management conditions, and health-service encounters; these were not counted as social determinants of health. Associations were reported across diabetes occurrence, diagnosis, management, complications, and quality of life. Biological and clinical factors were treated as correlates or stratifiers rather than social determinants of health. CONCLUSION: Across the EMR, diabetes was consistently reported in relation to material disadvantage, food insecurity, limited health literacy, constrained social support, and barriers to timely and continuous care. Behavioural factors and health-service encounters should be interpreted as pathways or contextual conditions, rather than SDH in isolation. The geographically uneven and predominantly narrative evidence supports policies that strengthen financial protection, health literacy, and equitable access to sustained diabetes care, alongside research from underrepresented countries.

title: A let-7a-5p-engineered extracellular vesicle-laden bioactive scaffold promotes immunomodulation and regeneration of segmental tracheal defects.
authors: Liu B, Wei N, Liang L, Shi Z, Liu P, Zeng T, Zhang H, Zhang H
abstract: Segmental tracheal defects resulting from trauma, tumor resection, or congenital malformations pose significant challenges for reconstruction. Persistent post-injury inflammation, inadequate neovascularization, and delayed epithelial restoration contribute to the formation of granulation tissue and subsequent graft failure. In this study, we developed a bioactive tracheal scaffold for sustained local delivery of let-7a-5p-engineered extracellular vesicles (let-7a-5p-EVs) to modulate the regenerative microenvironment during tracheal repair. The scaffold was constructed by integrating a mechanically optimized polycaprolactone (PCL) framework with a 20% Pluronic F127 hydrogel, which served as a local reservoir for EV retention and sustained release. Let-7a-5p-EVs were generated from lentivirally engineered human gingiva-derived mesenchymal stem cells and showed typical EV morphology, representative EV marker expression, and efficient uptake by airway epithelial cells. In vitro, let-7a-5p-EVs enhanced airway epithelial cell migration and shifted lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced macrophages from a pro-inflammatory M1-like phenotype toward a reparative M2-like phenotype, accompanied by reduced inflammatory cytokine expression. In a rabbit segmental tracheal defect model, the let-7a-5p-EV-laden scaffold enhanced neovascularization, mitigated local inflammatory responses, promoted mucociliary epithelial reconstruction, and maintained airway patency. The let-7a-5p-EV scaffold improved biomechanical recovery, and increased survival rates. Transcriptomic profiling and molecular validation indicated that these effects were associated with the attenuation of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)-associated inflammatory activation, as evidenced by reduced p65 phosphorylation and nuclear localization. These findings demonstrate that sustained local delivery of engineered EVs from a mechanically competent bioactive scaffold provides an effective immunomodulatory strategy for the regenerative repair of segmental tracheal defects and offers translational potential for functional airway reconstruction.

title: Serrated Pathway-Related Post-Colonoscopy Colorectal Cancer　Detected During Surveillance Colonoscopy: A Case Report.
authors: Hadatsuki H, Ichijima R, Mizuguchi Y, Toyoshima N, Okita H, Haga T, Kumamoto Y, Tsukamoto S
abstract: Post-colonoscopy colorectal cancer (PCCRC) remains a critical clinical challenge, and sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) are important precursor lesions. We report a case of advanced transverse colon cancer suspected to be associated with the serrated pathway that was detected during periodic surveillance colonoscopy. An 82-year-old male had undergone periodic surveillance colonoscopy after curative resection via endoscopic submucosal dissection for rectosigmoid intramucosal cancer. Colonoscopy revealed a type 2 advanced tumor near the hepatic flexure and multiple serrated lesions throughout the colon, fulfilling the diagnostic criteria for serrated polyposis syndrome (SPS). Immunohistochemistry showed deficient mismatch repair with loss of MLH1 and PMS2, and molecular analysis revealed BRAF V600E and KRAS mutations. The patient underwent robot-assisted transverse colectomy, and pathological staging was pT3N0. He remains recurrence-free 6 months after surgery. This case highlights the difficulty of distinguishing between a missed serrated lesion and a newly developed cancer in serrated pathway-related PCCRC. In patients with multiple SSLs or SPS, high-quality colonoscopy, recognition of SPS criteria, complete resection of detectable serrated lesions, and individualized surveillance strategies may be essential for the prevention and early detection of PCCRC.

title: CMKLR1 contributes to diurnal variation in brain injury after cardiac arrest by promoting lactate production in microglia.
authors: Li T, Fan Z, Wang H, Fan D, Peng F
abstract: Previously, the results of our clinical study have suggested that circadian rhythm have an impact on neurological outcomes following cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CA/CPR), but the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Here, using a mouse model of CA/CPR, we aimed to unravel the underlying mechanisms of the diurnal variation in CA/CPR-induced brain injury. The mice received 5 min of CA either in the active phase or in the inactive phase. To identify novel therapeutic targets for the impact of circadian rhythm on CA/CPR-induced brain injury, we applied high throughput RNA-seq analysis to profile mRNAs with differentially expression in the hippocampus of the two groups. Since it has been reported that CMKLR1 is beneficial for inhibiting neuroinflammation and improving neurological outcomes among many neurological diseases, we centered on this gene and clarified that its main cellular source is microglia. The correlation between CMKLR1 expression in hippocampus and neurological outcomes after CA/CPR was elucidated by CMKLR1 activation and knockout in microglia. The impact of CMKLR1 on microglial function, especially glucose metabolism, was clarified using BV2 microglia cell line by glucose uptake analysis, seahorse analysis and carbon 13 tracing. As a result, CA/CPR happening at active phase leads to better neurological outcomes with upregulation of microglial CMKLR1 in the hippocampus of mice. Our findings suggest that elevated microglial CMKLR1 expression in the hippocampus contributes to improved neurological outcomes after CA/CPR by promoting lactate production in microglia.

title: Hemodynamic effects of ventilating or not, during cardiopulmonary bypass in a porcine model.
authors: Kvalheim VL, Mongstad A, Husby P, Stangeland L, Nginamau ES, Osman TA, Yamada S, Grong K
abstract: Background. Optimal ventilator setting during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is unknown. Improved gas exchange and lung compliance have been suggested as favourable outcomes when lungs are ventilated. However, long-time effects have been hard to demonstrate. There has been less focus on the immediate circulatory effects of ventilator settings during cardioplegia and CPB, and potentially hemodynamic effects of different ventilator strategies are unknown. Methods. Sixteen anesthetized pigs on normothermic CPB with 80 min of aortic cross-clamp and cardioplegic arrest were randomized to a ventilated and a not ventilated group. After weaning, both cardiac-, hemodynamic-, and pulmonary functions were evaluated for up to 120 min. Results. Left ventricular variables and cardiac output did not differ between the two study groups, neither before nor after weaning. After weaning, mean pulmonary artery pressure was increased in ventilated compared to not ventilated animals. Neither pulmonary compliance nor oxygen uptake differed between groups in surviving animals. Conclusions. Disconnection of the ventilator during CPB and cardiac arrest did not affect lung compliance and oxygen uptake, neither positively nor negatively. In the ventilated group, a temporary increase in the pulmonary pressure after weaning was observed.

title: Multiple Rectal Neuroendocrine Tumors Treated by Endoscopic Resection: A Case Report.
authors: Matsuki H, Ichijima R, Sekiguchi M, Toyoshima N, Kawamura R, Mizuguchi Y, Takamaru H, Yamada M
abstract: Rectal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are typically solitary, and the occurrence of multiple lesions is uncommon. We present a case of multiple rectal NETs in a 41-year-old man. Colonoscopy performed at another hospital revealed three lesions (4 mm in the sigmoid colon and 5 and 10 mm in the rectum), all of which were diagnosed as NET, grade 1 (G1), following endoscopic resection; one lesion had a positive vertical margin. Upon referral to our institution, repeat colonoscopy demonstrated multiple yellowish, slightly elevated lesions throughout the rectum, all of which were histologically confirmed as NETs. Imaging studies showed no evidence of lymph node or distant metastasis. Although additional surgical resection was considered because of the multiplicity of lesions and positive margin, the patient strongly preferred endoscopic therapy. Eight lesions were successfully resected using endoscopic mucosal resection with a cap or endoscopic submucosal dissection. Histopathological examination revealed seven NET, G1 lesions and one NET, G2 lesion. Additional surgery was recommended but was declined by the patient, and no local recurrence or distant metastasis has been observed during 18 months of follow-up. This rare case highlights the potential role and the limitations of endoscopic treatment in patients with multiple rectal NETs.

title: Special Collection: Abstracts from IUNS-ICN Paris 2025
Cortical spreading depression on Riemannian 2-manifolds: eikonal-curvature analysis and sulcal trapping.
authors: Enver A, Tepe N, Sara MY, Dilekoz E, Bolay H
abstract: Cortical spreading depression (CSD) is a slowly propagating wave of near-complete neuronal depolarization underlying migraine aura and implicated in stroke, traumatic brain injury, and subarachnoid hemorrhage. Existing reaction-diffusion models of CSD treat the cortex as a flat Euclidean domain, ignoring its highly folded, individually variable geometry. We develop a fully covariant FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) reaction-diffusion system on a smooth compact Riemannian 2-manifold [Formula: see text] representing the cortical sheet, in which the Euclidean Laplacian is replaced by the Laplace-Beltrami operator [Formula: see text]. Three mathematical results are established: (i) local and global well-posedness in [Formula: see text] together with positive invariance of the physiological region via parabolic semigroup theory; (ii) a curvature-corrected eikonal relation [Formula: see text], in which the wavefront speed is modulated by the geodesic curvature of the front; and (iii) a sulcal-trapping theorem giving an explicit criterion under which an excitable wave entering a sulcus (negative Gauss curvature region) remains confined to it. Numerically, we develop two complementary solvers: a discrete exterior calculus (DEC) scheme on triangulated surfaces using the cotangent Laplacian with implicit-explicit (IMEX) time-stepping, and a physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate that evaluates [Formula: see text] via the closest-point projection of the ambient Euclidean Laplacian. The PINN framework supports both forward simulation and the inverse identification of excitability fields from sparse observations, and a noise-ablation study quantifies its practical identifiability. The parameters of the slow subsystem and of the coupling functions are inherited from our published, cohort-calibrated thalamocortical model, which was calibrated against 67 paired-pulse somatosensory evoked potential (SEP) recordings from nine analysable animals of a cohort of 14 male Wistar rats (1, 233 sweeps) acquired in the Neuroscience Laboratory of Gazi University, with CSD induced by topical KCl application. We validate convergence on [Formula: see text] with the spectral ground-truth [Formula: see text], exhibit a propagating ring wave with a refractory tail, and verify the eikonal-curvature prediction across two orders of magnitude in geodesic curvature, including the leading correction due to the recovery variable; a mesh-convergence study yields explicit resolution requirements for evaluating the trapping criterion on MRI-derived cortical surfaces.

title: Ground-truth benchmarking of signed, directed lagged connectivity: TemporalSignedMBB from a simulated gut-br​ain model to neural data.
authors: Purboyo TW
abstract: Methods inferring signed, directed, window-specific connectivity are rarely tested against a known answer. We benchmarked TemporalSignedMBB, which combines Gaussian conditional transfer entropy, tracking of edge-sign transitions, persistent homology and a Laplacian perturbation score, against planted ground truth: independent replications of a gut-brain model of depression, an inferential null, seven misspecified generators, heterogeneous subject-specific couplings and a Wilson-Cowan neural-mass model. Under correct latent specification, transfer entropy recovered planted directed couplings with precision 0.91 and recall 0.67 to 0.91; detected edges had correct signs in over 99.9% of cases. A cluster-robust edge test was calibrated under the null, but the realized false discovery rate was 0.09 at nominal 0.05, owing to subject-demeaning bias in short panels. Sign tracking detected 76% of true reversals with 5 false reversals in 180 network comparisons. Lag mismatch, saturating or abundance-scale coupling and latent drivers lowered recall to 0.46 or raised false discoveries to 0.19. Persistent homology missed planted directed loops that a directed cycle count detected, and the perturbation score did not predict perturbation responses. Individual networks recovered subject-specific couplings poorly, and with matched learners, network features gave case-control AUROCs of 0.56 to 0.59, against 0.97 to 0.98 for abundance features exploiting planted mean shifts, and 0.56 to 0.58 when groups differed only in coupling. In the neural-mass model, excitatory and inhibitory signs were recovered with an adequate lag order but not under volume conduction or hemodynamic observation. The results support group-level transfer entropy and sign tracking under favorable conditions, not the complete framework.

title: Hydrogen-rich saline alleviates inflammation-associated depression-like behaviors in mice.
authors: Fu ZJ, Ren ZY, He L, Zhang L, Wang Y
abstract: Despite the crucial role of inflammation in depression-like behavior, the low blood-brain barrier penetration of existing anti-inflammatory agents presents a substantial obstacle to effective treatment. Owing to the excellent blood-brain barrier permeability and anti-inflammatory ability of hydrogen-rich saline, this study explores its therapeutic effects on lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation-associated depression-like behavior in mice. In this study, mice intraperitoneally received lipopolysaccharide (0.83 mg/kg). Thirty minutes later, they intraperitoneally received hydrogen-rich saline (5 mL/kg). Results showed that hydrogen-rich saline significantly alleviated anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in lipopolysaccharide-treated mice, as assessed by open field tests, elevated plus maze tests, forced swim tests, and the tail suspension test. Peripheral inflammation was significantly reduced, associated with inhibited splenomegaly and decreased serum levels of interleukin-1β and tumor necrosis factor-α. Central inflammation was also decreased, related to the reduced number of activated microglia, inhibition of Tolllike receptor 4/myeloid differentiation primary response 88/nuclear factor-κB signaling, and repaired synaptic damage in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that early hydrogen-rich saline administration may attenuate lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation-associated depression-like behaviors, at least in part, by suppressing microglial pro-inflammatory activation and Tolllike receptor 4/nuclear factor-κB signaling.

title: Early self-regulation in context: Multidimensional organization of neonatal non-nutritive sucking and its association with subclinical maternal depressive traits.
authors: Faré O, Silvestri V, Morniroli D, Petrelli A, Colombo L, Giannì ML, Bulf H
abstract: From the very first days of life, infants' affective regulation unfolds within a dyadic co-regulatory system shaped by caregiver responsivity. In contexts of reduced maternal availability, such as maternal depressive states, infants may be required to compensate for diminished interpersonal regulation by increasingly relying on their internal resources. Neonatal non-nutritive sucking (NNS) represents one of the earliest spontaneously available regulatory behaviors, contributing to physiological and behavioral homeostasis from birth. However, it remains unclear whether its spontaneous organization is associated with early relational vulnerability indexed by maternal depressive symptoms. The present study aimed to characterize the spontaneous organization of NNS in a sample of newborns (N = 42) and to examine whether individual differences in NNS are associated with maternal postnatal depressive subclinical traits measured using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). Results from an exploratory principal component analysis indicated that neonatal sucking behavior was organized along two functional dimensions, reflecting overall sucking effort and behavioral activation, and the temporal organization of sucking bursts. Importantly, higher maternal depressive traits, though subclinical, were selectively associated with increased sucking effort, with infants of mothers reporting higher depressive traits showing more frequent and intense sucking, while no differences emerged for the organizational dimension. Overall, these findings suggest that individual differences in maternal depressive traits within the subclinical range may be associated with neonatal NNS effort, a precocious compensatory mobilization of regulatory resources, potentially serving both to support autonomous regulation and to elicit maternal engagement.

title: A psychedelic-rich alkaloid fraction obtained from Mimosa tenuiflora (Willd.) Poir attenuates somatic and affective symptoms of naloxone-precipitated morphine withdrawal in C57BL/6 mice.
authors: da Silva TR, Machado KLB, Carvalho IMM, de Sousa DC, de M Campos FD, da Silva GO, da L de Oliveira GAM, de Sousa RP
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Mimosa tenuiflora (Willd.) Poir. root bark is traditionally used in northeastern Brazil to prepare "Jurema wine", a beverage employed to relieve emotional distress and restore psychological well-being. However, validating its traditional preparations in central substance withdrawal states remains underexplored. AIM OF THE STUDY: To evaluate the ethnopharmacological potential of M. tenuiflora, we investigated the effects of an alkaloid fraction (AF II) from its root bark on somatic and affective morphine withdrawal symptoms in mice, without compromising analgesia. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Male C57BL/6 mice were used for the tests. Possible interference with morphine-induced analgesia was assessed using the acetic acid-induced writhing test. The animals were made morphine-dependent using a dose-escalation regimen, and withdrawal syndrome was precipitated with naloxone. AF II (3, 6, or 9 mg/kg, s.c.) was administered before withdrawal induction. RESULTS: AF II did not interfere with morphine analgesia. AF II significantly reduced key somatic signs of morphine withdrawal, decreasing jumping and paw tremor without affecting Walk in reverse. During withdrawal, AF II increased exploratory behavior in the open field and modulated anxiety-related parameters. CONCLUSIONS: The AF II from Mimosa tenuiflora, rich in serotonergic compounds, selectively attenuates somatic and affective components of opioid withdrawal in mice without compromising opioid analgesia, supporting its potential as a preliminary candidate for acute opioid withdrawal modulation. These findings provide scientific support for the traditional knowledge surrounding the central psychoactive and restorative properties of M. tenuiflora preparations.

title: Chaihu-Shugan-San attenuates depression by downregulating liver LCN2 to suppress LHb GluN2B-associated glutamatergic signaling.
authors: You X, Song C, Chen W, Zheng Y, Wang R, Liu W, Wei Y
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: The liver-brain axis has emerged as a critical pathway in depression pathogenesis, yet the molecular basis of this crosstalk remains largely unexplored. Chaihu-Shugan-San (CSS), a classic Traditional Chinese Medicine formula for "soothing the liver and relieving depression" has shown both hepatoprotective and antidepressant effects, but whether these actions are linked via the liver-brain axis and through what molecular mechanism remains unknown. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to determine whether CSS exerts antidepressant effects via the liver-brain axis and to elucidate the mediating role of liver lipocalin 2 (LCN2) and its receptor SLC22A17 in regulating lateral habenula (LHb) function. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model was established. CSS (2, 4, 8 g/kg) or fluoxetine (10 mg/kg) was orally administered. Depressive-like behaviors were assessed by sucrose preference, open field, and forced swim tests. Hepatic injury was evaluated by serum ALT/AST and H&E staining. Liver transcriptomics and LHb single-cell RNA sequencing were performed to identify key molecules, followed by qRT-PCR, Western blot, ELISA, and immunofluorescence for validation. The causal role of LCN2 was tested via liver-specific AAV-mediated overexpression. RESULTS: CSS ameliorated CUMS-induced depressive-like behaviors and liver injury. Transcriptomics and PPI network analysis identified Lcn2 as a hub gene. CSS reversed CUMS-induced elevation of LCN2 in the liver, serum, and LHb, as well as the upregulation of its receptor SLC22A17 in the LHb. LHb single-cell sequencing revealed that CSS restored CUMS-induced changes in astrocyte subcluster ASC6, including downregulation of AQP4 and SLC38A1 and impaired intercellular communication. Consequently, CSS reduced the elevated expression of c-FOS and GluN2B and restored AQP4 and SLC38A1 in the LHb. Importantly, liver-specific Lcn2 overexpression recapitulated CUMS-like depressive phenotypes and LHb abnormalities, including elevated SLC22A17 and GluN2B, and largely abolished the antidepressant effects of CSS. CONCLUSION: CSS ameliorates depressive-like behaviors in association with downregulation of hepatic LCN2 and its candidate receptor SLC22A17 in the LHb, restoring ASC6-mediated glutamate homeostasis, and suppressing GluN2B-related Glutamatergic Signaling. These findings are consistent with a model in which LHb function may be modulated via the liver-brain axis through hepatic LCN2 and its candidate receptor SLC22A17, although the direct source of LHb LCN2 remains to be determined, offering experimental support for the scientific basis of CSS in "soothing the liver and relieving depression."

title: Mechanisms underlying the effects of Buyang Huanwu Decoction against sepsis-induced ARDS using network pharmacology and experimental validation.
authors: Tan W, Wang C, Liu X, Deng J, Sang Z, Hu X
abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Buyang Huanwu Decoction (BYHW), a classic formula from Yilin Gaicuo Qing Dynasty, is indicated for stroke in patients with qi deficiency and blood stasis in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia. In traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), the pathogenesis of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is associated with qi deficiency, blood stasis, and heat-toxin obstructing the lungs, which align with the therapeutic actions of this formula. AIM OF THE STUDY: To investigate the effects of BYHW on sepsis-induced ARDS and the mechanisms underlying these effects. MATERIALS AND METHODS: ARDS was induced through LPS treatment in wild-type and eNOS-deficient (eNOS-/-) mice. The components of BYHW were analyzed using UPLC-UV-MS. Potential associated targets and pathways were predicted by network pharmacology and molecular docking experiments. Relevant protein and mRNA expression levels were assessed by Western blot analysis, immunofluorescence analysis, or qPCR. RESULTS: BYHW significantly improving the hypothermia, elevated plasma levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6, the lung index and injury induced by LPS in wild-type (WT) mice. However, these effects of BYHW were markedly in eNOS-/- mice. LPS downregulated AQP1 protein expression and upregulated Cav-1 protein expression and the p-P65/P65 ratio in both groups but increased the p-IκB/IκB ratio only in the WT mice. Pretreatment of BYHW increased the expression of eNOS and AQP1, decreased the Cav-1 expression and P65/IκB phosphorylation in WT mice, but the action on the P65/IκB phosphorylation and AQP1 expression were abrogated in eNOS-/- mice. CONCLUSION: BYHW protect against sepsis-induced ARDS may be related to decrease the eNOS-NF-κB-mediated synthesis of inflammatory cytokines and upregulation of AQP1 expression.

title: Integrated NeutroDrop-enabled single-cell ROS-NE droplet biosensing for sepsis auxiliary diagnosis and survival prediction.
authors: Yao Y, Wang F, Pu X, Shao M, Hua C, Cui J, Zhang Y, Wang Q
abstract: Sepsis assessment relies largely on organ-dysfunction scores and systemic biomarkers, which provide limited information on immune-effector function. We developed NeutroDrop, an integrated droplet microfluidic platform for single-cell profiling of neutrophil reactive oxygen species (ROS)-related oxidative activity and neutrophil elastase (NE)-associated proteolytic activity. Under standardized fMLP stimulation, individual neutrophils were co-encapsulated with fluorescent probes in monodisperse droplets, while membrane-integrity screening and software-assisted image analysis excluded multicell and membrane-compromised droplets. The study included 1012 neutrophils from 10 healthy controls and 2353 neutrophils from 20 patients with sepsis. Analysis of patient-level median signals showed reduced NE activity in sepsis (group means, 28.91 vs. 72.32), whereas ROS showed a nonsignificant decrease (72.14 vs. 92.26). Healthy-reference single-cell analysis revealed marked depletion of high ROS/high NE neutrophils in sepsis (2.89% vs. 16.86%), leading to the PerHighHigh index for healthy/sepsis classification. Local abundance analysis identified a data-derived low-amplitude ROS-NE region associated with non-survival; its patient-level abundance, Pi(R), stratified 12-day outcome with 83.33% sensitivity and 92.85% specificity in the discovery cohort. These locked rules were implemented in NeutroDrop-Plus, which correctly classified all 10 operator-blinded samples and matched 12-day outcomes in 5 of 6 sepsis cases. NeutroDrop converts neutrophil single-cell functional heterogeneity into quantitative biosensing indicators for adjunctive sepsis classification and exploratory short-term outcome stratification.

title: Dissolvable sacrificial interfacial shielding for stable microneedle arrays-based electrochemical dynamic monitoring of sepsis-associated lactate.
authors: Chen WX, Lin CH, Lu YR, Lu TC, Chen ZH, Saqib M, Lei Y, Liu AL
abstract: Continuous lactate dynamic monitoring is essential for timely clinical intervention in sepsis, yet existing serum-based assays are invasive and inherently unsuited for real-time measurement. Microneedle array electrodes (MAEs) enable minimally invasive in situ lactate monitoring in interstitial fluid (ISF); however, mechanical wear at the electrode-tissue interface remains a major obstacle to stable and reproducible analysis. Herein, we report a dissolvable polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP)-shielded MAE for reliable lactate dynamic monitoring. The device integrated an epoxy resin/multi-walled carbon nanotubes microneedle core with a lactate oxidase-gelatin/polythiophene-citrate (LOx-GEL/PEDOT-COO-) sensing interface, combining mechanical robustness, conductivity, biocompatibility, and selective lactate sensing. In artificial ISF, the sensor showed a linear amperometric response from 0.25 to 32 mM with a detection limit of 0.14 mM. Importantly, the dissolvable sacrificial PVP layer was introduced to preserve enzyme activity before use, reduce mechanical abrasion during skin insertion, and subsequently dissolve in situ to enable effective analyte access. In a sepsis-relevant hydrogel skin model, the resulting MAE-based biosensor demonstrated stable and continuous lactate dynamic monitoring, confirming its practical applicability. This dissolvable interfacial shielding strategy provides a versatile design framework for enhancing durability, sensing reliability, and operational safety in microneedle-array enzymatic electrochemical biosensors for ISF biomarker dynamic monitoring.

title: Polaris: A toolkit for standardized construction, integration, and quantitative testing in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
authors: Xie R, Wang R, Zhan Y, Wei B, Xu S, Chen Y, Liu L
abstract: Existing synthetic biology toolkits have expanded part libraries and assembly capabilities. However, new users may still encounter ambiguity in construct definitions, hierarchical transitions, genomic integration routes, and quantitative testing procedures. Here, we present Polaris, a Golden Gate toolkit for Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Polaris uses a MoClo-derived three-level hierarchy. Level 1 stores reusable parts, Level 2 generates transcription units and other intermediate constructs, and Level 3 supports multigene assembly and switching between testing and integration backbones. The toolkit distinguishes part interfaces from transcription unit interfaces, uses BpiI and BsaI in successive assembly stages, and provides parallel ccdB and mScarletI3 screening options. Integration modules and quantitative characterization frameworks were implemented in both hosts and demonstrated using representative genetic parts and activation and repression systems. A companion digital platform further encodes the Level 1 to Level 3 rules for assembly planning. Polaris connects hierarchical construction, stable genetic implementation, and quantitative testing within a common execution framework, providing a practical basis for data accumulation, part standardization, and future automation.

title: Integrated distal enzyme engineering and intrinsically disordered peptide fusion enable efficient (-)-Germacrene D biosynthesis in Serratia marcescens.
authors: Xia B, Hu X, Wang L, Yang T, Zhou X, Wu S, Fan TP, Cai Y
abstract: (-)-Germacrene D is a bioactive sesquiterpene with demonstrated insect-repellent and behavioral regulatory activities. Here we report an integrated three-pronged strategy combining distal enzyme engineering, intrinsically disordered peptide (IDP) fusion, and pathway-level regulation to boost (-)-germacrene D production in the terpene-tolerant chassis Serratia marcescens HBQA7. A semi-rational distal mutagenesis pipeline-integrating spatial shell stratification, ConSurf conservation filtering, and Pythia folding ΔΔG screening-identified 58 candidate sites from 411 distal residues and yielded the double mutant XsGDSV52E/C183V with 2.5 g L-1 of (-)-germacrene D. N-terminal fusion of the NEXT IDP tag, selected from eight candidates, increased (-)-germacrene D production to 5.3 g L-1 without increasing the intrinsic catalytic efficiency of GDS. Promoter-based regulation of mvk using a stationary-phase promoter library further increased the titer to 6.3 g L-1. Fed-batch fermentation at the 5 L scale ultimately delivered 46.1 g L-1 of (-)-germacrene D with a glucose conversion yield of 16.2% (w/w)-the highest germacrene-type sesquiterpene titer reported to date.

title: ROS-responsive Se@HSC-DIA enables local drug delivery and modulates CD44high inflammatory nucleus pulposus cell states in intervertebral disc degeneration.
authors: Huang Y, Su M, Li M, Chen Z, Xu B, Chen Y, Lin T, Chen R
abstract: Low back pain is closely associated with structural abnormalities of the spine, yet how altered mechanical loading drives persistent disc inflammation and pain remains unclear. Here, we investigated the cellular mechanisms linking structural disturbance to intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) and developed a mechanism-guided local therapy. Human disc specimens from patients with lumbar spondylolysis (LS), integrated single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, primary nucleus pulposus cells (NPCs), pharmacological perturbation, and an in vivo IVDD model were analyzed. LS-associated discs showed increased NOX4 and CD44 expression with enhanced oxidative stress and inflammation. Single-cell analysis identified a CD44high inflammatory NP population (Inflamed NP) that expanded with degeneration severity. Oxidative stress promoted this state, whereas IL-1β-IL-1R1 signaling and canonical NF-κB activation sustained its inflammatory and matrix-catabolic phenotype. Drug screening identified diacerein (DIA) as an effective inhibitor of this axis. We therefore developed Se@HSC-DIA, an injectable hydrogel that responds to reactive oxygen species (ROS) and integrates CD44 affinity, ROS-triggered DIA release, and selenium nanoparticle-mediated antioxidant activity. Se@HSC-DIA reduced ROS, NF-κB activation, inflammatory mediators, and matrix catabolism in NPCs. In vivo, it preserved disc structure, restored matrix homeostasis, alleviated pain-related behavior, and shifted the degenerative transcriptome toward homeostasis without evident systemic toxicity. These findings define a ROS-IL-1β/IL-1R1-NF-κB axis linking structural stress to an inflammatory NP state and support microenvironment-responsive biomaterials for IVDD therapy.

title: Environmental Impact of Conventional Versus Underwater Endoscopic Mucosal Resection for Colorectal Lesions: A Procedure-Based Life Cycle Assessment With Pooled Effectiveness Estimates.
authors: Calabrese G, Moll F, Neves JAC, Bonacci L, Sinagra E, Castiglione F, Maida M, Albéniz-Arbizu E
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The environmental impact of endoscopic techniques remains poorly defined. We compared procedure-related environmental outcomes between conventional endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) and underwater EMR (U-EMR) for colorectal lesions. METHODS: In this prospective pilot procedure-based life cycle assessment of the resection phase, 10-25-mm colorectal lesions underwent EMR or U-EMR across three endoscopy units. Outcomes included global warming potential (GWP, kg CO2-equivalent/procedure), waste, life-cycle water consumption, fossil resource scarcity, and terrestrial acidification. Exploratory GWP per en bloc resection was estimated using pooled randomized-trial and pilot-cohort data. RESULTS: Forty-nine procedures were included: 23 EMR and 26 U-EMR. En bloc resection was achieved in 56.5% of EMR and 69.2% of U-EMR, and R0 resection in 52.2% and 69.2%. Mean GWP was significantly lower with U-EMR than EMR (1.92 ± 0.54 vs. 2.42 ± 0.50 kg CO2-eq; p = 0.002), corresponding to a reduction of 0.50 kg CO2-eq per procedure and 50 kg CO2-eq per 100 procedures. U-EMR was associated with lower waste generation (324.0 ± 78.3 vs. 407.3 ± 72.0 g; p < 0.001), water consumption (0.56 ± 0.17 vs. 0.77 ± 0.20 m3; p < 0.001), fossil resource scarcity (0.33 ± 0.10 vs. 0.40 ± 0.09 kg oil-eq; p = 0.007), and terrestrial acidification (0.0052 ± 0.0018 vs. 0.0068 ± 0.0018 kg SO2-eq; p = 0.003). Findings were consistent across scenario and uncertainty analyses. In the meta-analysis-based model, GWP per en bloc resection was lower with U-EMR than EMR (2.59 vs. 3.51 kg CO2-eq), corresponding to a 26.3% relative reduction. CONCLUSIONS: U-EMR was associated with lower procedure-related environmental burden than conventional EMR, persisting after normalization for en bloc resection. TRIAL REGISTRATION: No. 165/26.
